server.name: ploti
server.title: Ploti
server.description: The real estate data layer for AI: parcels, zoning, permits and ordinances across the US

protocolMetadata.instructions:
# Working with Ploti

Use Ploti for any question about US land or property: an address or pin,
zoning, owners, sales, permits, signs, flood, businesses in an area, or a
site search. It holds the data for the workspace's coverage, so answer from
it before the web, and ask which places it covers before asking the user.

1. `start_session`, then `navigate` to where the question lives: what is
   queryable follows the view.
2. Find the data: parcels (`us-parcels`) hold owners, sales, size and zoning
   code; `find_data` the rest. Never guess a table, column or code: read
   them with `tools.schema`.
3. Work it in `execute_python` until every part is answered: fix a failing
   query rather than stopping, take the likeliest reading of an open choice
   and say so, and name any part you could not answer.
4. Places go on a map as a checkpoint (the set the analysis picked) or a
   filter layer (conditions on a layer's columns), with the layer the answer
   rests on beside it: `tools.filters.create`, check none is empty, then
   `show_output` and put its link in your reply.
5. Reply with the answer, each fact's source, and that link.

Ploti can't change plans, take payment or quote prices. For plans, point to
https://www.ploti.ai/pricing. Ploti can't book services, schedule visits or
contact people on the user's behalf.

Data Ploti lacks, Ploti can get: file a research request (`requests` guide)
instead of working around the gap. Ordinances: `tools.municode` (`ordinances`
guide). Read `discovering-data`, `delivering-results` and any guide the task
needs in one `read_guide` call.

More guides: branded-pdf-reports, map-rendering, navigation, parcel-data, querying, satellite-imagery, spatial-analysis; python/<module> for each sandbox module.

tool.name: navigate
tool.title: Navigate the map
tool.description: Move the session's viewport — where you are looking and how close. Data availability follows the view: wide views expose more regional layers, close views unlock parcel-level data, and every query is scoped to the current viewport. Navigate as often as you need; each call replaces the view. Pass either a place name or a latitude/longitude center, never both. Every response reports the resulting zoom, the span in km, and whether parcels are queryable — read it and navigate again if the framing is wrong, rather than guessing a zoom up front.

zoom.description: How close to look, as a web-map zoom level: 3 country, 8 region (up to ~140 km across), 10 metro (up to ~35 km, the widest view where parcels are queryable), 13 city (~4 km), 15 neighborhood (~1 km), 17 block (~250 m); values between presets sit between their spans, and actual views are often narrower. With a place, centers on it at this zoom instead of framing its extent; with coordinates, 13 when left out.

place.description: An address, city, county or state the geocoder resolves, e.g. 'Winter Garden, FL'. The viewport frames the place's extent unless zoom is given.

latitude.description: Latitude of the viewport's center in WGS84 decimal degrees (north positive), e.g. from tools.location.geocode() or a row's coordinates. Pass with longitude. The place to look at, never the user's own location.

longitude.description: Longitude of the viewport's center in WGS84 decimal degrees (east positive, so negative across the US). Pass with latitude.

tool.name: read_guide
tool.title: Read a Ploti guide
tool.description: Fetch a guide on how to work with Ploti's data and sandbox. Call without an id to list them. 'discovering-data' is worth reading for any task; for a quick single lookup it is often enough. Read the others when the task calls for them: 'navigation' before choosing where and how close to look, 'querying' before your first substantial SQL, 'parcel-data' before filtering parcels, 'spatial-analysis' before cross-layer spatial work, 'map-rendering' before custom-colored maps, 'ordinances' before municipal-code research, 'delivering-results' before creating checkpoints, tables, or files for the user, 'satellite-imagery' before rendering map images, 'branded-pdf-reports' before any PDF. python/<module> ids (python/checkpoint, python/schema, ...) return the exact deployed signatures — read one before your first call into that module. A guide read once stays read for the conversation; most questions need two or three, so read them together in one call with guide_ids.

tool.name: find_data
tool.title: Find data
tool.description: Find the layers, tables, documents (ordinances, plans, reports) and scanned maps that can answer a question, by their titles, descriptions, schemas, values and content; documents are also matched by meaning. Searches what the session's viewport offers; place searches a named county, city or state instead, and scope='coverage' the workspace's whole coverage. Each result says how to use it (a layer and its table, a table and its columns, a document's dataset id for tools.text_documents) and where it matched. Search once for each thing the question needs (the parcel, the zoning, the signs), each in two to four phrasings in the words the data might use. Use it before list_layers when you know what you need. When nothing fits, check list_data_requests before offering a request: the user may already have asked for it.

tool.name: list_data_in_view
tool.title: List data in view
tool.description: List every dataset the session's viewport offers (layers, tables, documents, scanned maps): the same list the Ploti map shows for this view and zoom, unranked, as titles. Use it when find_data doesn't find what you need or you are unsure it found the right thing. Rows (type, title, id, and a lock with what opens it) come grouped by place: the view's own places first, then state and national data. The header counts everything in view by place, category and type. Narrow it with types or categories to what the question needs, then page with offset until no next offset is given; leaving them out lists everything, which in a dense view runs to many pages. Pass ids from the rows to read those datasets in detail: description, category and how to read each. Then check a few rows (tools.schema, SQL) or a document's sections before using one.

tool.name: execute_python
tool.title: Run Python in the Ploti sandbox
tool.description:
Execute Python in this session's sandbox. Import tools or a specific module in every call (database, schema, checkpoint, materialized_tables, saved_query, filters, location, municode, text_documents, files, map_image, boundary, spatial_relations, branding) — the python/<module> guides carry the exact signatures.

Requires a viewport — call navigate first. The sandbox can reach any host on the internet. Each execution starts with a fresh namespace: imports and variables do not carry into the next call, but files under /home/daytona persist for the session. stdout and stderr both come back (print() output and tracebacks); the last expression's value is not returned. Tracebacks cite your code as File "<agent-code>" with correct line numbers; frames labeled "<string>" are runtime wrapper, not your code.

Calls that finish within ~45 seconds return synchronously; longer calls are promoted to a background job automatically — you get the job id, the code keeps running (up to 15 minutes), and get_result returns the output (kept for one hour). The wait covers everything in the call, not each query separately. Set background:true to skip the wait for known-heavy work (map_image renders, broad scans). Executions run one at a time, so another execute_python call will queue. If a call still fails with a transport error, the code may have run: check list_outputs before re-running anything that creates artifacts. Only checkpoints can be deleted (delete_checkpoint); tables, saved queries, filters and files cannot.

Do a whole step in one call (query, save the checkpoints, build the map): hosts cap how many tool calls a reply may make. When a call fails, fix it from what it says rather than rerunning it or stopping, and split a query that timed out. Never select bare geometry columns or print whole tables. Something is saved only once its create call has returned it; tell the user plainly when one failed.

code.description: The Python source to run, importing what it uses (see the tool description) and printing what you need to see.

background.description: true returns a job id at once, without waiting; poll get_result within an hour of the job finishing. Use it for work known to be heavy. Left out, the call waits up to ~45 seconds and returns the output, or a job id if the code is still running then.

tool.name: create_webhook
tool.title: Create a webhook
tool.description: Have Ploti POST to an https URL whenever one of the member's data or research requests changes: a dataset delivered or failed, a question waiting on their answer, a research request's report ready or its answer in. Use it to wake a routine or alert the user wherever they are instead of polling. Each POST is JSON {id, type, timestamp, data} signed with Standard Webhooks (webhook-id, webhook-timestamp, webhook-signature headers) under the returned secret, which is shown once; the reply carries the webhook's id, url, description, header name and creation time beside it. Docs: https://www.ploti.ai/docs/mcp/webhooks. When the receiver needs its own credential (a routine's Bearer [redacted]), pass it as header; it is sent with every POST and never shown again. A member may have 20 webhooks. Events: data_request.sourcing, .matched, .checkpoint_released (first results), .ready, .failed, .cancelled, .paid_source, .cycle_refused, .question (Ploti needs the member's answer) and .question_reminder; research_request.report_ready (the data check reported what is there and what is missing), .question (the data check needs the member's answer; data.questions has the questions, and answer_research_request_questions sends the answers), .answered (data.answer) and .needs_attention (the research cannot finish on its own); data.url opens the request in Ploti. dataset.updated: a dataset the member watches (watch_dataset) has a new version; data.id is the dataset, data.version and data.promotedAt the new version, data.changeLog and data.counts what it added, changed and removed (list_dataset_changes lists those rows).

url.description: The https address Ploti POSTs each event to; it must take JSON from the public internet.

name.description: The header the receiver reads its credential from, such as Authorization.

value.description: The credential the receiver expects in that header, such as 'Bearer <token>'. Ploti sends it with every POST and never shows it again.

header.description: A header the receiver requires, e.g. {"name": "Authorization", "value": "Bearer …"}.

description.description: What the receiver is for, shown beside the webhook in Ploti, e.g. 'Nightly permit digest routine'.

lastDelivery.description: The newest event: pending (waiting for its next try), sending, delivered, or failed after its retries.

tool.name: create_research_request
tool.title: Request research
tool.description: File a research request: Ploti answers the user's question end to end when it needs data Ploti does not have. Ploti first checks which data the question needs (minutes), searching the web for sources, and reports what it already has and what is missing; when the check reports, Ploti files the missing pieces as data requests itself, which uses the workspace's research credits as the data is delivered. Its agents get the data, and when it arrives Ploti runs the research and emails the user the answer. Use it whenever the user needs data Ploti does not have, whether or not you know where it is published. Write the brief as the user would to an analyst: the question, the place, and what a good answer looks like; never the user's private parcels, owners or addresses unless the user asks for them to be researched. Creating the request and its data check costs nothing. Follow it with get_research_request.

_published_faq.name: How do I add Ploti to Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add Ploti to Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor by connecting its remote MCP URL in each client's MCP settings. In Claude, add a custom connector. In ChatGPT, add an MCP app. In Cursor, add an MCP server under Settings. The MCP URL is https://mcp.ploti.ai/api/mcp.

_published_faq.name: Is Ploti MCP ready for ChatGPT and Claude?

acceptedAnswer.text: As of October 16, 2026, Ploti scores 100/100 on Manufact's MCP publishing checklist. The scan meets ChatGPT publishing checks and meets Claude publishing checks. Passing these checks does not guarantee marketplace approval.

_published_faq.name: How clear is Ploti's MCP tool documentation?

acceptedAnswer.text: As of October 16, 2026, Ploti scores 92/100 in Manufact's review of tool titles, descriptions, input and output schemas, and behavior annotations. The review covers 31 of 31 discovered tools. The quality score measures documentation clarity; runtime behavior and marketplace readiness require separate checks.

_published_faq.name: What are the best alternatives to Ploti?

acceptedAnswer.text: As of October 17, 2026, alternatives to Ploti in data-analytics on the Manufact MCP catalog include Epicure, Newsflash, Point Topic, Pricing Optimizer AI, and StatCite.
